transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doc, it's... it's these darn small spaces. What brings me in is that whenever I step into a slow elevator or, you know, a small locked room, my chest just jumps right away. I get this strong need to get back out before I can even think straight. It's like my whole body is telling me to run. Which reminds me, the other day I was at the hardware store—the one down on Elm Street, you know the one? They used to have the best prices on nails, back when I was building that shed in the backyard. Took me three months to finish that shed. My grandson helped me paint it, though he got more paint on his overalls than the wood. Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the elevator there is so slow, and I just couldn't do it. Had to take the stairs, and my knees aren't what they used to be, let me tell you.
Do you ever feel this kind of anxiety or fear in situations that aren't small or enclosed spaces?

No, no, it's pretty much just those tight spots. I mean, I know a little storage room or... or that elevator over at the museum isn't the same as being actually locked up, you know? But my mind just treats it like trouble the minute I see there's no window and the door shuts tight. 

We were at that museum just a couple weeks ago, actually. Took my youngest granddaughter to see the dinosaur bones. She's absolutely crazy about the T-Rex, reads all the books about 'em. Anyway, they had this gift shop at the end of the tour, and let me tell you, they charge an arm and a leg for these little plastic toys now. Ten bucks for a dinosaur no bigger than my thumb! When I was a kid, you could get a whole handful of tin soldiers for a nickel down at the five-and-dime. We used to line 'em up on the porch railing and knock 'em down with rubber bands. My brother Charlie had a real good aim with those... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the anxiety. Yeah, no, I don't really get that feeling out in the open or anywhere else. Just when I'm boxed in.
Do you ever have episodes where you suddenly feel intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes?

Out of nowhere? Like a sudden... peak, you said? No, no, I don't get anything like that. Unless I'm looking at a tiny closet or a stuck elevator, I'm as calm as a cucumber. I don't just get scared out of the blue. I can just be sitting in my recliner watching the television, totally fine. 

I was watching *The Price is Right* just this morning, actually. You know, Drew Carey does a fine job, but he's no Bob Barker. Bob had that... that real presence, you know? And he always reminded you to spay and neuter your pets at the end. I always told my late wife, Martha, that if we ever went out to California, we'd get tickets to that show and wear matching shirts. We never did make it out West, though. Farthest we ever got was Chicago for my nephew's wedding back in '92. He married a lovely girl, big Italian family. The food at that reception, let me tell you... they had this pasta dish with the little clams in it, and a whole roast pig! I must have eaten my weight in garlic bread alone. My stomach wasn't too happy with me on the drive back, but it was worth it. 

Wait... what did you ask me? Something about feeling uncomfortable? Yeah, no, I don't get those sudden feelings you're talking about. Just the tight spaces.
Is your anxiety always triggered by being in a small or enclosed space?

Oh, absolutely. Every time. It's always those small spaces that do it. Like... well, like my buddy Earl's car. He had one of those old Volkswagen Beetles back in the seventies. Tiny little thing. I tried getting in the back seat once and my chest just about exploded, had to make him pull over before we even got out of the neighborhood. 

Earl loved that car, though. Painted it bright yellow. Looked just like a rolling lemon going down the street. We used to take it down to Miller's Pond to go fishing on the weekends. The bass fishing was real good back then, let me tell you. We'd use these special lures Earl made himself out of old bottle caps and chicken feathers. He was a real crafty guy, Earl. Built his own mailbox that looked exactly like a little red barn, complete with a tiny silo and everything. The mailman got a real kick out of it until some teenagers knocked it over with a baseball bat one Halloween... 

Now, why did I bring up Earl? Oh, right, your question. Yeah, if it's a tight, enclosed space like that back seat or a little room, it gets me every single time. But outside of those tight spots? I'm right as rain.
Does the anxiety occur even if you're in a large space but feel enclosed, such as being in a big room with no clear exit?

No, no, if it's a big room, I'm fine. Even if the doors are shut or whatever, as long as I can stretch my arms out and there's space around me, it doesn't bother me. It's just the... the squeezing in, you know? Like feeling the walls right up against your shoulders. 

Speaking of big rooms, they held the town hall meetings in the old high school gymnasium when they were trying to pass that new zoning law. Biggest room in the county, I reckon. The bleachers were still pulled out, the same ones I used to sit on when I watched my boy play basketball back in... oh, must have been '84. He had a wicked jump shot, my son. Number 32. They went all the way to the state semi-finals that year. Course, the uniforms were a lot shorter back then, those little shorts they wore. Looks ridiculous now when you see the pictures, but that was the style. The coach, Mr. Henderson, he used to pace up and down the sidelines chewing on a wet cigar. Never lit it, just chewed it down to a nub by the fourth quarter. 

But anyway, yeah, the gymnasium. Even with all those people packed in for the town hall, shouting about property taxes, I didn't feel panicky at all. So no, big rooms are fine. It's just the little spaces.
Is it the lack of windows or the doors being shut that bothers you in these small spaces, or is it just the overall feeling of being in a tight area?

Well, it's... it's a bit of both, I suppose, but mostly the doors and windows. Or the lack of 'em, I should say. I know a little storage room or an elevator at the museum isn't the same as being locked up, but my mind treats it like trouble the minute I see there's no window and the door shuts tight. It's like... click. That's it. 

We had this storage room down in the basement of the hardware store I used to work at. Old Mr. Higgins owned the place. He was a good man, but cheap as the day is long. Wouldn't pay to put a proper lightbulb in there, just had this little pull-string thing that barely gave off a glow. You'd go down there looking for a box of galvanized nails or some copper piping, and you could smell the damp, you know? Like old wet cardboard and mouse droppings. Higgins had this orange tabby cat named Marmalade that was supposed to take care of the mice, but that cat was lazier than a hound dog on a porch in August. Just slept on the bags of fertilizer all day. 

I remember one time, the delivery boy—what was his name? Tommy? Timmy? Timmy, that's right. He had freckles all over his nose. Anyway, Timmy accidentally locked me in that basement storage room for a good ten minutes before he heard me hollering. Boy, I gave him an earful when he finally opened that door. 

But yeah, what were we talking about? Oh, the tight areas. Right. It's the door shutting. If there's no window and the door closes, my brain just says, "Nope, we're in trouble now."
Is it ever the thought of being in a small space, rather than the actual physical space itself, that triggers your anxiety?

Well, no, not really just the thought of it. If I'm sitting in my living room watching the television and I think about an elevator, I don't get all worked up. It's when I'm actually there, looking at the doors about to close. 

Speaking of television, you know what they used to show on Sunday afternoons? Those old Westerns. Bonanza, Gunsmoke. Now that was good television. Not like the garbage they have on now with all the yelling and the... the reality shows or whatever they call them. My wife, Mary, God rest her soul, she loved James Arness. Said he was the handsomest man on television. We had this big console TV, one of those wooden ones that looked like a piece of furniture, you know? Took up half the wall. Had to get up and turn the dial to change the channel. Course, we only had three channels back then anyway, so it wasn't much trouble. Sometimes the picture would get all fuzzy and you'd have to mess with the rabbit ears, maybe put a little tin foil on the tips. 

But no, just thinking about a small room doesn't bother me none. I gotta be standing in it, or right about to step inside, before my heart starts doing somersaults.
Do you often avoid entering small spaces or take steps to avoid being in them because of your anxiety?

Well, yeah, I do try to steer clear of them if I can help it. These days I take the stairs instead of the elevator, or I'll pass on those archive jobs down in the basement at the museum. Sometimes I even ask a friend to wait nearby if I absolutely can't avoid a closed-in place, even though I feel a bit foolish doing it. 

Speaking of the museum, they got this new exhibit on local history. Real fascinating stuff. They dug up some old farming equipment from out near Miller's Creek. The plow they have on display, it looks just like the one my grandfather used to use. He had a pair of mules, Buster and... oh, what was the other one's name? Blue! Buster and Blue. Meanest mules you ever did see. If you didn't watch your step, Blue would give you a kick that'd send you flying into next week. My granddad, though, he had a way with them. He'd just whistle this little tune, sounded kind of like a meadowlark, and those mules would settle right down. He grew the best sweet corn in the county, my granddad did. Used to sell it out of the back of his pickup truck on Saturdays. A dollar a dozen, if you can believe that. Try getting a dozen ears of corn for a dollar nowadays. You're lucky if you can get two for that price at the supermarket. And it doesn't even taste the same. It's all... I don't know, watery. 

But anyway, yeah, I avoid those little spaces. Just easier that way, you know? Taking the stairs keeps the legs strong, anyway.
Does avoiding small spaces ever cause problems for you in your daily activities or relationships?

Well, I suppose it causes a few hiccups here and there. I've had to turn down some of the docent tasks at the museum, and I've skipped a few gallery events because I just don't want to get stuck dealing with those closed-in rooms or having to take the elevator up to the third floor. It hasn't stopped my whole life, but it has made my volunteering and outings a bit more limited than they used to be. 

You know, speaking of the museum, they used to have these wonderful little galas on the top floor. Fancy affairs, with little sandwiches with the crusts cut off and those little meatballs on toothpicks. Mary and I used to go to those. She'd wear this lovely pearl necklace her mother gave her. Real pearls, none of that plastic junk you see nowadays. Her mother, she was a character. Lived to be ninety-two, and she smoked a pack of Pall Malls every single day. Always had one hanging out the corner of her mouth while she played solitaire at the kitchen table. She'd shuffle those cards like a professional dealer in Las Vegas. Never been to Vegas myself. Too loud, too many flashing lights. I prefer a quiet evening on the porch, maybe listening to the crickets. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, problems. Yeah, it's just... I miss out on some things at the museum, that's all. It's a shame, but I just can't bring myself to go in those little rooms.
Is it ever the physical presence of someone with you in a small space that makes you feel less anxious?

Well, I can't say it does. Having somebody standing right there next to me in a tiny room... it doesn't really make the walls feel any wider, you know? I'm still just as antsy. 

Though, speaking of being stuck with folks in tight spots, I remember riding all the way down to Florida in the cab of a '68 Chevy pickup with my buddy Arthur. Now that was a tight squeeze. Three grown men on a single bench seat, 'cause his brother-in-law came along too. Arthur, he always smelled like peppermint and motor oil. He was a mechanic down at the old Sinclair station on 4th Street. Back when they actually pumped your gas for you, washed your windshield, checked your tire pressure. Proper service, you know? You don't see that anymore. Now you gotta stand out in the freezing rain and do it yourself, and the pump is blaring at you with some little TV screen playing advertisements. Who in their right mind wants to watch a commercial while they're pumping gas? It's just noise, everywhere you go, just noise. 

Arthur could fix anything, though. Give him a wrench and a piece of wire, he'd have an engine purring. Cars were simpler then. You could actually open the hood and recognize the parts. Nowadays, it's all computers and plastic covers. You gotta plug a car into a laptop just to figure out why it won't start. Makes no sense to me. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, having company. No, having a buddy with me doesn't do a lick of good for the nerves. I just want out of there, no matter who's standing next to me.

You don't see that anymore. Now you gotta stand out in the freezing rain and do it yourself, and the pump is blaring at you with some little TV screen playing advertisements. Who in their right mind wants to watch a commercial while they're pumping gas? It's just noise, everywhere you go, just noise. 

Arthur could fix anything, though. Give him a wrench and a piece of wire, he'd have an engine purring. Cars were simpler then. You could actually open the hood and recognize the parts. Nowadays, it's all computers and plastic covers. You gotta plug a car into a laptop just to figure out why it won't start. Makes no sense to me. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, having company. No, having a buddy with me doesn't do a lick of good for the nerves. I just want out of there, no matter who's standing next to me.
